extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in psychology of motivation and humor (and theoretically-minded comedians/writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Apter's Reversal Theory to analyze or design humorous stimuli by evaluating metamotivational state, the presence and structure of cognitive synergies, arousal, and framing. The rubric is specific to identifying when play-oriented (paratelic) processing enables delight in simultaneous opposite readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition 1: perceiver is in the paratelic state
rubrics_metrics.description: The perceiver is in the paratelic state (playful, present-focused, activity-as-its-own-goal) or the stimulus successfully induces it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paratelic persons seek and enjoy arousal; activities are intrinsically valued. For humor to occur the audience must either already be paratelic (e.g., relaxed, playful context) or the joke must shift them into that state. Anti-patterns: audiences who are anxious, goal-focused, or task-driven (telic) will not experience the stimulus as humorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition 2: a cognitive synergy is present
rubrics_metrics.description: A cognitive 'synergy' — one thing possessing two opposite qualities at the same time — must be present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: a toy gun (weapon + not-weapon), a pun (word with two opposing meanings), a metaphor (A is and is not B), a dignified person behaving absurdly. The synergy is the structural basis of the joke: an object/sentence/situation must legitimately support two conflicting readings simultaneously. Evaluators should check that both readings are salient and intelligible to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition 3: the synergy is held simultaneously (not resolved)
rubrics_metrics.description: The cognitive synergy must be held simultaneously rather than resolved into a single reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor depends on keeping both (or multiple) contradictory readings active at once; if the ambiguity resolves cleanly into one interpretation the humorous tension collapses. Anti-patterns: punchlines or explanations that eliminate ambiguity rather than sustaining the dual readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition 4: high arousal accompanies perception
rubrics_metrics.description: High arousal must accompany the perception of the synergy — the experience is felt as exciting/intense rather than calm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the paratelic state arousal is sought and experienced as pleasurable; the synergy should produce felt intensity. If arousal is low the stimulus may be merely odd; if arousal is experienced as threatening it produces anxiety, not humor. Consider physiological or reported excitement as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diminishment direction (humor-specific synergy)
rubrics_metrics.description: For humor specifically, the synergy typically contrasts a serious/important reading with a diminished (less important/less real/less powerful) reading held together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of a serious reading being reframed as not-serious/diminished produces comedic effect. Examples/applications: cartoons of powerful figures (powerful reading + diminished depiction), pratfalls of pompous characters (status + humiliation). Check whether one reading represents seriousness and the other reframes it as trivial or unreal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective frame must be in place
rubrics_metrics.description: A protective frame is required so that arousal is experienced as play rather than threat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames can be physical (a comedy club), conventional (this is fiction/a joke), or relational (trusted friend). Without an adequate frame the same stimuli elicit anxiety rather than enjoyment. When designing/evaluating humor, verify cues that establish safety and non-danger (audience expectations, setting, signals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions / anti-patterns: situations that preclude humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations that fail to meet the above conditions are unlikely to be humorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically: (a) stimuli that don't induce or find the audience in a paratelic state (audience too anxious or task-focused); (b) synergies that resolve too cleanly so only one reading survives; (c) lack of a protective frame so the violation feels real. Use these as disqualifiers when diagnosing failed jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic checklist (evaluation questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of practical diagnostic questions to evaluate whether a stimulus will function as humor under Reversal Theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions listed: Is the audience in or shifted to the paratelic state? Does the stimulus contain a real cognitive synergy (one thing with two opposing qualities at once)? Is the synergy in the diminishment direction (serious → not-serious)? Is a protective frame in place? Does arousal feel exciting rather than threatening? Use these as an ordered checklist when analyzing or designing comedic material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telic vs. paratelic characterization (the central reversal)
rubrics_metrics.description: People oscillate between telic (serious, goal-directed, arousal-avoidant) and paratelic (playful, present-focused, arousal-seeking) metamotivational states; humor requires or induces the paratelic pole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This core theoretical distinction explains why identical stimuli may be experienced as nuisance/annoyance in telic mode but delightful in paratelic mode. When evaluating humor, characterize audience motivational state and whether the material is framed to encourage paratelic processing.
